risks.title: Pressure vessel rupture / shrapnel
risks.condition: The rocket and GSE contain gas and saturated N2O at high pressure (tank pressures 425-1050 psi across the operating temperature range) within weight-optimized structures.
risks.departure: A pressurized component ruptures or a fitting/hose lets go, projecting shrapnel or releasing a cutting jet of escaping fluid.
risks.asset_text: Personnel near the pad or test setup; vehicle and GSE hardware.
risks.consequence: Penetrating/laceration injuries from shrapnel or gas momentum; destroyed flight hardware.
risks.description: Keep all persons clear of the system whenever N2O or other pressurized gas is present anywhere other than the supply bottle; slowly open fittings to relieve trapped pressure keeping hands away from escaping gas; whip-check lines that may whip when vented; enforce minimum standoff distances (500 ft for L-M class).
risks.source_note: 1.4.1: 'High pressure can cause hardware to break, projecting shrapnel in any direction at high velocities... escaping fluid acts like a knife or a bullet.'

risks.title: Stuck pressurized oxidizer tank
risks.condition: The oxidizer run tank can trap pressure if control of the vehicle valves is lost after fill.
risks.departure: A sealed, pressurized oxidizer tank cannot be commanded to depressurize and must be approached or forcibly vented.
risks.consequence: Prolonged hazardous condition on the pad; potential rupture if unrelieved.
risks.description: A static vent (small hole, typically .020-.047" diameter) at/near the top of the N2O volume is a built-in leak: even in the event of total control failure the rocket will always depressurize itself given enough time (est. 1-1.5 hours for a full tank); staged 100/50/20-ft listening approach before anyone closes with the vehicle.
risks.source_note: 1.4.1: 'Even in the event of total control failure, the rocket will always depressurize itself... because the static vent is a built-in leak'; 7.5.2 boil-off and approach protocol.

risks.title: Fuel fire at the pad
risks.condition: Flammable liquid fuel (E85/alcohol/kerosene) and pyrotechnic igniters are handled and loaded during vehicle preparation, and dumped propellant can pool at the pad after an abort.
risks.departure: Free fuel is ignited by open flame, sparks, or another ignition source and the fire spreads from a puddle or leak.
risks.asset_text: Personnel, vehicle/GSE hardware, and nearby equipment, structures, or vegetation (brush fire).
risks.consequence: Burn injuries; hardware damage; secondary fires of surrounding equipment or vegetation.
risks.description: Keep open flame, sparks, and ignition sources away when handling fuel, especially with a known spill or suspected leak; keep a Class B extinguisher or bucket of water/sand on hand; let fires burn out with personnel at a safe distance unless very small and safely extinguishable; mop up non-evaporating hydrocarbon fuel after a dump.
risks.source_note: 1.4.2: 'Fires can occur when free fuel is ignited and spread rapidly if there is a puddle or leak present.'

risks.title: N2O venting onto ignition sources
risks.condition: N2O is an oxidizer that splits into nitrogen and oxygen and accelerates any fire it feeds.
risks.departure: N2O is vented near hot parts, embers, sparks, or open flame, or is mistakenly used on a fire, intensifying combustion.
risks.consequence: Rapid fire acceleration and escalation of an otherwise minor fire.
risks.description: Do not vent N2O near hot parts, embers, sparks, or open flame; N2O must NEVER be used to fight fires despite appearing cold; keep all persons clear of the system when N2O is present anywhere other than the supply bottle.
risks.source_note: 1.4.3: 'N2O will accelerate fires... N2O should NEVER be used to fight fires.'

risks.title: Contained N2O decomposition
risks.condition: N2O decomposes exothermically above ~1000°F (threshold lowered by catalysts such as fine metal particles/contaminants), and adiabatic compression in fast-acting valves or cavitation can locally reach that temperature.
risks.departure: Contained N2O decomposes, producing a rapid pressure spike and free hot oxygen that combusts with anything flammable.
risks.asset_text: Personnel near the system; oxidizer tank, plumbing, and vehicle.
risks.consequence: Tank/line explosion with simultaneous oxidizer-fed fire; potentially lethal to anyone nearby.
risks.description: All N2O valves other than the supply bottle valve are actuated remotely when N2O is present; no N2O pumps around personnel; keep all persons clear of the system when N2O is present anywhere other than the supply bottle.
risks.source_note: 1.4.4: 'decomposition temperature is normally around 1000°F, but a catalyst... can lower that threshold'; adiabatic compression in solenoid/poppet valves cited as most common trigger.

risks.title: Delayed decomposition after a fire
risks.condition: A fire occurring around a vessel containing N2O gas — even at ambient pressure — can heat residual vapor toward decomposition.
risks.departure: Personnel approach a rocket or tank after a fire, and lingering heat triggers a delayed decomposition/tank explosion.
risks.asset_text: Personnel approaching the vehicle after an anomaly; surrounding vegetation (brush fire risk while waiting).
risks.consequence: Tank explodes long after the initiating event, injuring responders.
risks.description: No persons may approach a rocket, test setup, or any other N2O tank for a minimum of two minutes following the last indication of fire or smoke unless thoroughly purged with inert gas (CO2); NEVER approach a burning N2O tank — leave it to burn out; have emergency fire response available if vegetation ignition is a risk.
risks.source_note: 1.4.4: 'no persons may approach... for a minimum of two minutes following the last indication of fire or smoke'; 'approaching an inflamed N2O rocket is more hazardous than leaving it alone.'

risks.title: BLEVE on sudden tank failure
risks.condition: The run tank holds saturated liquid N2O under pressure.
risks.departure: A sudden large leak or bulkhead tear-out causes the liquid to flash to gas — a Boiling Liquid Expanding Vapor Explosion (BLEVE).
risks.asset_text: Hardware and anything within debris-throw radius.
risks.consequence: Explosive energy release beyond an equivalently sized pressurized-gas container; increased damage and projected debris distance (almost certainly secondary to an initiating failure).
risks.description: Keep all persons clear of the system when N2O is present anywhere other than the supply bottle; standoff distances sized to total stored propellant energy.
risks.source_note: 1.4.5: 'a BLEVE will almost certainly not be the primary hazardous event... but it will increase damage to hardware and the projected distance of any thrown debris.'

risks.title: Confined fuel-air explosion
risks.condition: Fuel vapor and N2O gas can accumulate in confined, stagnant volumes during fueling or from gross leaks.
risks.departure: A fuel-air (or fuel-N2O) mixture reaches the explosive threshold in a confined space near an ignition source and detonates.
risks.asset_text: Personnel and structures in the confined space.
risks.consequence: Detonation causing blast injuries and structural damage.
risks.description: Handle fuel only in well-ventilated areas (near an open roll-up door or outside) — solvent fuels evaporate slowly and disperse readily, making explosive mixtures unlikely in ventilation; keep all persons clear of the system when N2O is present anywhere other than the supply bottle.
risks.source_note: 1.4.6: 'The only real risk... is when a gross leak of both fuel and N2O gas occurs in a confined space near an ignition source.'

risks.title: Inadvertent e-match initiation / electrical fire
risks.condition: The system uses large low-voltage batteries, high-voltage sparker circuits, and electric initiators (e-matches).
risks.departure: A short, induced current, or stray charge fires an initiator or starts an electrical fire while personnel are close (e.g., hands near the nozzle during igniter hookup).
risks.asset_text: Personnel handling igniters and avionics; vehicle wiring and GSE.
risks.consequence: Unintended pyrotechnic event — flame/hot gas exposure, burns; electrical shock; equipment fire.
risks.description: Keep e-matches and initiators shunted (leads twisted) until connection; always spark-check electrical leads (briefly touching supply wires together) before connecting initiators; keep high-voltage devices powered down until needed; insulate exposed wires; keep hands and body clear of the nozzle when connecting igniter leads.
risks.source_note: 1.4.7/1.4.8: 'Always spark-check electrical leads... before connecting initiators'; 'keep hands and other body parts clear of the nozzle.'

risks.title: Burn from hot components or accidental pyro discharge
risks.condition: The thrust chamber assembly retains substantial heat for several minutes after firing, and pyrotechnic materials can ignite when mishandled.
risks.departure: A person touches a hot component or is exposed to flame/hot gas from an accidental pyrotechnic ignition.
risks.asset_text: Personnel recovering or servicing the vehicle.
risks.description: Feel for radiant heat with the back of the hand ~1/2 inch from the surface before quick-touch testing; cool hot metal with a small amount of water; keep hands clear of the nozzle during igniter lead connection; spark-check leads first.
risks.source_note: 1.4.8 and 7.6: 'the thrust chamber assembly may be very hot after firing... place the back of your hand about half an inch away.'

risks.title: N2O cold burns on skin contact
risks.condition: Parts recently exposed to liquid N2O are extremely cold, and liquid N2O can escape at fittings (especially supply-bottle-to-hose and hose-to-fill-valve) when venting or loosening them.
risks.departure: Escaping or residual liquid N2O contacts skin, its rapid boiling absorbing heat from the tissue.
risks.asset_text: Hands and exposed skin of personnel venting or disconnecting fittings.
risks.description: Keep hands and exposed skin away from the fitting being loosened; quick-touch feel cold parts to test temperature before handling.
risks.source_note: 1.4.9: 'The rapid boiling of escaping liquid will absorb heat from anything it touches, which can cause frostbite.'

risks.title: N2O fume inhalation indoors
risks.condition: Liquid fuels are volatile and continuously evaporate; cleaning agents and motor exhaust are also airborne chemicals.
risks.departure: Fumes build up in a closed room and are inhaled in quantity.
risks.description: Handle fuels only in well-ventilated areas (near an open roll-up door or outside); as a general rule avoid breathing any airborne chemicals.
risks.source_note: 1.4.10: 'the fumes must build up in a closed room... only handling fuels in well-ventilated areas.'

risks.title: Asphyxiation from large indoor gas release
risks.condition: N2O and CO2 can rapidly displace air in a closed volume, and a warm bottle moved to a cold environment can develop a hand-valve leak from thermal contraction.
risks.departure: A large gas release indoors displaces breathable air.
risks.asset_text: Personnel in the room (including a vehicle interior).
risks.consequence: Drowsiness up to asphyxiation from oxygen deficiency.
risks.description: Work with compressed gases only in well-ventilated areas; if a bottle leaks indoors, immediately evacuate, open doors/windows, close the bottle or take it outside, and run fans; always ensure bottle hand valves are fully tightened, especially when moving a warm bottle into an air-conditioned car or room.
risks.source_note: 1.4.11: 'Venting a large volume of non-air gas in a closed room may result in drowsiness, or at an extreme, asphyxiation.'

risks.title: Premature approach to an energized vehicle
risks.condition: The igniter can fail to light the motor after oxidizer fill, or the vehicle valves can fail to open, leaving a loaded, armed rocket on the pad (hang-fire condition).
risks.departure: Personnel approach the loaded vehicle too soon, or a transmitter power-cycle energizes the igniter circuit and commands the valves open, causing accidental ignition/launch with people downrange.
risks.consequence: Accidental ignition and launch, or exposure to a pressurized oxidizer-loaded vehicle at close range.
risks.description: Load-and-go opens the vehicle valves to dump all propellant even if ignition does not occur; if valves cannot be opened, wait out static-vent boil-off (at least one hour for a full tank, est. 1-1.5 hours total) with a staged 100/50/20-foot listening approach, never approaching closer than 100 ft while venting is audible; DO NOT power-cycle the transmitter (boot requires switches UP, energizing igniter and valves); after three failed remote valve attempts, turn the transmitter off and leave it off until fully safed.
risks.source_note: 7.5.2: 'this may take anywhere from a few minutes to over an hour... DO NOT turn the transmitter off and back on... could result in accidental ignition and launch.'

risks.title: Recovery deployment failure / ballistic descent
risks.condition: The recovery system depends on pyrotechnic deployment events, shear pins, shock cords, and parachutes that degrade with use.
risks.departure: Drogue or main fails to deploy, the airframe fails to separate, or a worn shock cord snaps, resulting in a ballistic or partially-slowed return.
risks.consequence: High-speed impact — ballistic return is treated as a heads-up event that can pose a risk to people and property; propulsion section free-fall and major hardware damage.
risks.description: Dual redundant deployment controllers each with drogue and main charges, continuity-checked before launch; conservatively sized, ground-tested ejection charges and shear pins; parachute-cannon packing arrangement; shock cord replacement schedule (5 launches uninsulated); if separation is not confirmed at apogee, notify the RSO of a possible ballistic return and put all persons in bunkers; heads-up calls for rockets descending near people; bunkers at FAR for experimental launches.
risks.source_note: 7.4.6: 'Always treat an unseparated rocket as a heads-up event that can pose a risk to people and property in the vicinity'; 2.7: worn shock cord 'can snap during deployment.'

risks.title: Inadvertent initiation during handling
risks.condition: Personnel are present near the vehicle during transport, handling, and pre-launch preparation while it contains fuel and pyrotechnic igniter materials (no oxidizer loaded).
risks.departure: An inadvertent initiation occurs during handling — noting that unlike a solid motor, a standard liquid motor cannot be ignited by accident during transport, handling, or pre-launch preparation (fuel sealed in the tank, no oxidizer loaded); the credible events are limited to pyrotechnic e-match/ejection-charge initiation.
risks.asset_text: Personnel transporting and preparing the vehicle.
risks.consequence: Localized burns or pyrotechnic injury rather than motor ignition.
risks.description: Fuel is sealed in the tank and oxidizer is never loaded until all personnel are clear; e-matches and charges kept shunted until connection; spark checks before connecting initiators; deployment controllers armed only when a launch window is imminent.
risks.source_note: 1.4: 'a standard liquid motor simply cannot be ignited by accident during transport, handling or pre-launch preparation; for one, its fuel is sealed away inside the tank, and secondly, no oxidizer is loaded.'

risks.title: Recovery crew field injury
risks.condition: Recovery operations take place on foot in desert terrain, often in extreme heat, with hot/cold vehicle components at the landing site.
risks.departure: Recovery personnel suffer heat illness, dehydration, wildlife encounter, or contact injury from extreme-temperature components.
risks.consequence: Severe dehydration and rapid-onset heat exhaustion (danger 'cannot be overstated' above 110°F); burns/frostbite; snakebite or terrain injury.
risks.description: Buddy system (at least two people) for recovery; dress for the weather and carry plenty of water; caution regarding rough terrain and venomous wildlife; radiant-heat/quick-touch checks before handling components.
risks.source_note: 7.6: 'when temperatures exceed 110° F, the danger posed by severe dehydration and rapid-onset heat exhaustion cannot be overstated.'
risks.watch_observable: Launch-day forecast temperature and recovery-area terrain/wildlife report
risks.watch_threshold: Forecast above 100 °F or recovery area beyond 1 mi from vehicle access
risks.watch_contingency: Delay recovery until evening; assign a two-person recovery team with water and first-aid kit.
